1:
Clarke thinks the chapter opens in the wrong place: the first verse should end the preceding chapter and this one begin with the second, since as it stands the sense is not consistent. His remedy is grammatical: the opening verb can be read as a future rather than a past, the prefixed Hebrew conjunction being often conversive, so the sentence joins the end of the previous chapter and runs, the Lord hath called Bezaleel and Aholiab and filled them with wisdom, and they shall work, and every wise-hearted man in whom the Lord put wisdom. Ellicott treats the verse as introductory to something much larger, a section reaching to the close of the thirty-ninth chapter, stating in brief that the workmen accomplished what Moses had committed to them according to all that the Lord commanded.

Ellicott and Calvin then face the obvious objection, that the section merely repeats instructions already given. Ellicott grants that it is little more than a repetition of the earlier chapters, differing only in recording as done what had been ordered, and finds the minute exactness deliberate, teaching that acceptable obedience is a complete and exact observance down to the smallest point. Calvin defends it at greater length. Moses might seem prolix, but he repeats the narrative almost word for word by design, so that it could be seen by actual comparison how exactly the artificers conformed to the pattern. This was not merely a commendation of obedience: nothing human was to enter the structure, and however strenuously each man exerted himself he might not give the slightest scope to his own inventions, which would have profaned the building; the repetition would also restrain later generations from altering anything. They did not understand the reason of every number and measure, he adds, but it became them to be sure God had commanded nothing without purpose.

Henry reads the opening as a lesson in the use of gifts: when God had qualified them, then they applied themselves, and talents entrusted to us are not to be laid up in a napkin but traded with. On the calling he is careful: even those whom God has qualified must wait for a regular call, and Moses called precisely those in whose heart God had put wisdom beyond their natural capacity and whose heart stirred them up in earnest, so that ability and willingness together are what to look for in the call of ministers. Wesley reproduces that judgment almost word for word and adds the same conclusion, that men are called to build the gospel tabernacle whom God has by grace made fit for the work and free to engage in it. Gill adds that qualifications were not enough, and that all concerned in the public service of the church should have a call both from the Lord and from the church.

On the arrangements Gill speculates carefully. When they began is not said, though probably they set about it as soon as they had materials; nor is it said where they wrought, but likely there was a particular place where the craftsmen were ranged by trade under the direction of the two men named. Ellicott fills in what was handed over — gold, silver, bronze, acacia wood, thread and goats’ hair, skins, stones, oil and spices. Calvin turns to the source of the skill, noting how often Moses exalts the grace of the Spirit in the workmen’s ingenuity: he first calls them skilful architects, then corrects himself by adding that they were furnished from above. From this Calvin argues against those who cite such passages to prove free will, since even where a will is right it is foolish to infer that it proceeds from the man himself; the same holds of the eagerness with which each contributed labour or substance, which Scripture assigns to the gift of the Spirit.
3:
The verse divides into a handing over and a continuing inflow, and the commentators take one or the other. Gill follows the materials into the workshop: Bezaleel and Aholiab received the offering from Moses and distributed it to the several workmen as the nature of each man’s task required, gold to some, silver, brass or fine linen and dyed yarn to others, and acacia wood to others again. He adds a note on Moses himself, that he gave out faithfully everything he had received and kept back nothing for his own use or private advantage. Ellicott takes up the second clause. The liberality of the people did not stop when the work was taken in hand; they kept bringing fresh offerings morning after morning until the workmen found there was more than enough. He sets two later parallels beside it, the giving when David was collecting materials for the temple, and the giving when the second temple was about to be reared after the return from captivity.

Keil and Delitzsch work on the report that follows. The wise workmen came, each from the work he was making, and told Moses that the people were bringing much more than sufficed for the labour of the work, the preposition in the phrase being comparative; whereupon Moses had proclamation made through the camp that no one was to prepare anything further from his own property as a holy heave-offering, and with that he stopped any further giving.

Calvin reads the whole scene as a display of three virtues and then of one warning. Prudence appears in the distribution of the materials among the workmen; diligence in the quickness with which they began without waiting until they had enough to finish; and integrity, most of all, in their volunteering that enough had been given and putting a stop to the offerings before they exceeded what was needed. Few men restrain themselves, he observes, when an opportunity of undetected thieving is offered, and even where there is no disposition to deceive most people are tempted by ambition to want more passing through their hands than they need.

The people’s part strikes Calvin harder still. They were not rich, having had no long period in which to lay up treasure, and the wealthiest among them had no more than what had been carried secretly out of Egypt, while the building was sumptuous; yet they did not stop contributing beyond what was necessary until an edict forbade them. Such promptitude deserved no common praise, which is what makes it the more astonishing that the same people should soon afterwards neglect the God whose service they were so zealous in and fall into gross idolatry. Calvin draws two conclusions from the contrast: that the zeal which existed in them for a short time came from the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and that all our best feelings vanish unless the gift of steadfastness is added to them.
4:
The episode is short and the readers mostly admire it. Gill identifies the men who came as the ingenious craftsmen employed on one part or another, whether on the tabernacle itself or on its vessels and furniture, and has one of them speak in the name of the rest. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the wording of the proclamation. Moses forbade anyone to make any more property for a holy heave-offering, that is, to prepare anything further out of his own goods to offer for the building; and the closing statement that the material was enough and to spare uses a word for their sufficiency, with the addition rendered literally as leaving some over. From that they draw the covenant sense of the episode: by so liberal a contribution of freewill gifts for the work the Lord had commanded, the people proved their willingness to uphold their covenant relationship with their God.

Clarke is struck by the rarity of the situation. He notes what a liberal spirit these people show, and that Moses was obliged to issue a proclamation to stop them because there was already more than enough. From that he argues to the character of the man in charge. Had Moses been intent on gain, or anything less than perfectly disinterested, he would have encouraged the flow and multiplied gold, silver and precious stones to himself; that he did not is ample proof that he sought no secular advantage but was doing the Lord’s work under the inspiration of the Divine Spirit. Clarke then generalises: everything necessary for the worship of God will be cheerfully provided by a people whose hearts are in that worship. He goes further and turns the observation on his own country’s arrangements, arguing that where the laws tolerate every form of worship it would be well to find some less exceptionable way of providing for the national clergy than by tithes — let them have the provision the law allows, but not by a method that exposes them to the resentment of their flocks, alienates affection and injures their usefulness.

Ellicott reads a detail out of the wording of the prohibition. Since Moses forbids any man or woman to make any more work for the offering, it would seem that the superfluous offerings were chiefly things produced by labour — thread, goats’ hair yarn and the like — so that the humblest class of contributors appears to have been the most zealous. He ends with a question rather than a comment, asking when Christian liberality will ever be so excessive as to need restraining. Gill keeps to the plain sense of the last verse, that the gold, silver, brass and precious stones, the wood and the yarn already brought in were sufficient for everything they had been ordered to make.
8:
Gill marks the change of subject. From this point to the end of the chapter the narrative is simply an account of the making of the tabernacle — its curtains, coverings, boards, sockets and bars, the veil for the most holy place and the hanging for the entrance — exactly as they had been ordered to be made, so that he refers the reader back to his own comments on the earlier chapter rather than repeat them. He notes that each man did the part assigned him, whatever he was fittest for and most skilful in, and that some made the ten curtains which were properly the tabernacle and were made first, the other things following. He also observes a peculiarity of the telling: throughout the account it is said that he did this and that, which may refer to Moses by whose order the things were done, or to Bezaleel as chief director of the work, or to each craftsman severally.

Keil and Delitzsch answer that question grammatically. The verbs through this section are third person singular with an indefinite subject, corresponding to the German man or the French on — so the singular is impersonal rather than a hidden name. They also set out the structure of what follows, dividing it into the hangings and covering, the wooden boards and bars, and the two curtains with the pillars, hooks and rods that supported them, and noting that each answers to a section of the earlier instructions; since those have already been explained, nothing further needs saying about them here.

Henry reads the fabric itself. The first work undertaken was the framing of the house, which had to be done before its furniture could be prepared, and this house was made not of timber or stone but of embroidered curtains coupled together. That, he says, typifies the state of the church in this world. Though it stands on the earth its foundation is not in the earth as a house’s is, since Christ’s kingdom is not of this world nor founded in it. It is mean and mutable and in a militant state: shepherds dwelt in tents and God is the Shepherd of Israel, soldiers dwelt in tents and the Lord is a man of war whose church marches through an enemy’s country and must fight its way, and while the kings of the earth enclose themselves in cedar the ark of God was lodged in curtains only. Yet there is a beauty in holiness, and the curtains were embroidered as the church is adorned with the gifts and graces of the Spirit. And the several societies of believers are united in one, as here all the pieces became one tabernacle, for there is one Lord, one faith and one baptism.

Clarke takes up the one technical term. The word rendered cherubim probably means no more than figures of any kind, worked in the loom in diaper fashion, or embroidered with the needle, or cut with the chisel or graving tool in wood, stone or metal; and he reports that able critics have contended for that sense. In some places, he grants, the word seems restricted to a particular figure then well known, but in many others it appears to mean any figure commonly produced by sculpture, carving, engraving or weaving. On the measurements that follow he refers the reader back to the earlier chapter, as Gill does.
14:
Henry is the only commentator to stop over the coverings, and he reads them as two lessons in one. The curtains of hair-cloth spread over the tabernacle, with the covering of rams’ skins and badgers’ skins above them, signify to him the shelter and special protection the church is under. God has provided for his people a shadow from the heat and a covert from storm and rain; they are armed against all weathers, so that the sun and the moon shall not smite them; and they are protected from the storms of divine wrath, that hail which will sweep away the refuge of lies. Those who dwell in God’s house will find, he says, that however violent the tempest or however continual the dropping, it does not rain in.

The second lesson he takes from the framework beneath. The boards and bars that bore the curtains up signify the strength and stability of the church, which for all that is still only a tabernacle. He presses the construction itself: the boards were coupled together and joined by the bars that shot through them, and it is the union of the church, and the hearty agreement of those who are its stays and supporters, that contributes so abundantly to its strength and establishment. The image works both ways — a tent that cannot be leaked into, and a frame that holds only because its parts are pinned to one another.
30:
Only Ellicott has anything of substance here, and what he has is textual. On the sockets he says that under every board two sockets is undoubtedly the true meaning, but that it can scarcely be got out of the text as it stands: the Hebrew phrase for under the one board ought to have been repeated twice, as it is in the corresponding verse of the earlier chapter, and in one of the two places it has accidentally dropped out. The claim is a small one but a definite one — not a difficulty of sense but a copying loss, and identified by comparison with the parallel passage rather than by conjecture.

On the sides he corrects the rendering instead. Where the English speaks of the sides westward, Ellicott would read the back of the tabernacle westward, and refers the reader to his note on the same phrase in the earlier chapter. Clarke, for his part, does no more than point back to his own comment on the making of the bars, which is his practice throughout the remainder of the chapter.
35:
Henry reads the two hangings as a pair of lessons about access, and begins from the building trade. In the raising of any house, he observes, there is a great deal of work about the doors and the partitions; and in the tabernacle these answered to the rest of the fabric, since it was a structure of cloth throughout, so that curtains served for doors and a veil for a partition where another building would have used timber or a leaf of stone. The first was made to divide the holy place from the most holy, and Henry takes that division to signify two things at once: the darkness and distance of that dispensation compared with the New Testament, which shows the glory of God more clearly and invites us to draw near to it, and the darkness and distance of our present state compared with heaven, where we shall be ever with the Lord and see him as he is. The second veil was for the door of the tabernacle, and there the people assembled even though they were forbidden to enter. Henry makes that arrangement the point rather than the restriction: a congregation gathered at a door it may not pass is doing what it can, and while we are in this present state, he says, we must get as near to God as we can.

Wesley takes over the first half of that reading almost word for word, giving the veil between the holy place and the most holy the same double sense — the comparative darkness and distance of the older dispensation set against a New Testament that shows the glory of God more clearly and invites us near, and the darkness and distance of our present state set against a heaven where we shall be ever with the Lord and see him as he is. He stops there, without adding the observation about the outer door, so that in his hands the verse carries the doctrine of the two dispensations and nothing else. Clarke adds nothing beyond a pointer back to his own note on the veil in the earlier chapter, which is his practice with every remaining item here; the whole weight of comment on the veil in this chapter therefore rests on one reading, repeated by two hands.
37:
Clarke closes the chapter with a general observation rather than a comment on the hanging or its pillars, for which he refers the reader back to the earlier chapter, glossing only the hooks of the five pillars as their capitals. There is scarcely anything in the chapter, he says, that has not been touched already, since this and the remaining chapters of the book are in general a repetition of what has been met in detail from the twenty-fifth chapter onwards. He then gives the reason the repetition is not waste. God had commanded the work beforehand, and it was necessary to record its execution in order to show that everything was done according to the pattern shown to Moses; without this detailed account we should not have known whether the work was ever carried out as directed.

He adds one note that concerns the margins rather than the text. At the head of the chapter he has advanced the dates of the world and before Christ by a year without altering the year of the exodus, which he acknowledges may look at first sight like an error; the explanation is that those two reckonings begin at Tisri while the years of the exodus are dated from Abib, so the two scales part company for part of the year.
